title: 1963 Ankara mid-air collision
summary: Middle East Airlines Flight 265, a Vickers Viscount descending for approach to Ankara from Cyprus collided at 7,000 feet with a Turkish Air Force Douglas C-47 on a training flight. The Viscount pilot had misestimated his position relative to navigation fixes and failed to maintain proper radio contact with Ankara Air Traffic Control. Both aircraft fell directly onto a residential neighborhood. All 17 occupants of both aircraft and 87 people on the ground were killed.
probable_cause: The Viscount pilot incorrectly estimated the distance between navigation fixes, failed to comply with international standards for radio communications, and failed to follow the planned instrument flight rules procedure by flying under visual flight rules instead.

title: Aeroflot 191
summary: Aeroflot Flight 191, an Ilyushin Il-18V on a domestic Soviet flight with a stopover, was landing at Ashgabat when a dust storm deteriorated faster than forecast. The crew received an initial weather forecast indicating sky covered by cumulonimbus clouds with 600-1000m cloud base and 4-10 km visibility, with dust storm expected after 21:00. However, weather worsened much faster and at 17:00 new data indicated dust storm with 300m visibility and strong winds, which was not communicated to the crew.
probable_cause: The immediate cause was flying in violation of minimum weather standards. Air traffic controllers were blamed for not providing updated weather information or offering alternate airport. The crew was also faulted for not seeking updated weather information, though strong radio interference prevented them from hearing ATC weather reports. The radio compass gave false readings due to atmospheric interference.

title: Aeroflot 25
summary: During climb from Moscow to Krasnoyarsk, the No. 4 engine malfunctioned and initiated reverse thrust, creating severe drag on the right wing. Pilots feathered both right propellers because they could not determine which engine was responsible. The severe drag caused a sharp descent; aerodynamic loads tore off both ailerons, and the aircraft plummeted to the ground at 500-600 km/h.

title: Mohawk Airlines 121
summary: Mohawk Airlines Flight 112 attempted takeoff on runway 28 into a heavy thunderstorm on 2 July 1963. The co-pilot was unable to maintain control as the wind had shifted from a headwind to a tailwind. The aircraft fell to earth two minutes after takeoff, struck the ground left wing-first, cartwheeled wing-over-wing and caught fire. The Civil Aeronautics Board found the cause to be the pilot's decision to take off in bad weather.

title: New Zealand National Airways Corporation 441
summary: A Douglas DC-3 Skyliner operating Flight 441 from Auckland to Tauranga flew into a vertical rock face in the Kaimai Ranges at 2,460 feet altitude on 3 July 1963 at approximately 9:09 am NZST. The Civil Aviation Authority investigation found that a downdraft carried the aircraft below the level of the range crests into an area of extreme turbulence from which the crew could not recover altitude. The investigation noted that under very poor weather conditions and probably unaware of their true position, the crew initiated a premature descent to the officially designated minimum safe altitude for the area. Another aircraft was caught in strong downdrafts the same day but managed to recover. Twenty-two of the 23 people aboard were killed instantly; one person survived the impact but died shortly afterward. Three extra passengers who were supposed to be on the flight changed their plans at the last minute.
probable_cause: A downdraft carried the aircraft below the level of the crests of the range into an area of extreme turbulence from which recovery of altitude was impossible under the prevailing poor weather conditions. The crew was probably unaware of their true position and initiated a premature descent.

title: United Arab Airlines 869 (1963)
summary: United Arab Airlines Flight 869, a de Havilland Comet 4C, reported being overhead Santa Cruz VOR at 7,000 feet at 1:46 am and was cleared to descend to 4,000 feet. The crew reported encountering severe turbulence and requested a left-hand approach procedure rather than the standard right-hand approach due to weather. At 1:50 am, the aircraft entered the left-hand turn in severe turbulence and heavy rain and crashed into the Arabian Sea 9 nautical miles from Madh Island. The investigation concluded the aircraft was probably lost due to loss of control while turning in severe turbulence and heavy rain, as no wreckage was salvaged and the crew reported no problems before impact.

title: Swissair 306
summary: Flight 306 took off from Zurich in dense fog and reached 2700 meters altitude four minutes after takeoff. A white trail of smoke was observed from the left side of the aircraft, followed by a long flame from the left wing. The aircraft entered a gentle left turn and began descending more steeply into a final dive. A Mayday was issued and the aircraft crashed near Dürrenäsch. The accident resulted from overheated aircraft brakes during taxiing through fog at full engine power, causing magnesium wheels to burst.
probable_cause: Aircraft brakes overheated from application of full engine power during taxiing to disperse fog. Magnesium wheels burst, with one bursting on the runway before departure. When landing gear retracted after takeoff, hydraulic lines in the gear bay were damaged by burst wheel rim fragments. Spilled hydraulic fluid ignited when contacting overheated landing gear rims, causing fire in the gear bay that spread to the wing. The resulting electrical problems and structural damage led to loss of control.

title: 1963 BAC One-Eleven test crash
summary: The prototype BAC One-Eleven crashed 23 minutes after takeoff from Wisley Airfield on October 22, 1963, killing all seven crew on board. The aircraft was conducting stall tests at 16000 feet with flaps extended 8 degrees when it entered a stable stall and descended at high rate in horizontal attitude. The wings blocked airflow over the elevators causing a deep stall from which recovery was impossible. The aircraft broke up on impact at Cratt Hill near Chicklade. This was the first accident attributed to the deep stall phenomenon, which led to adoption of stick-shakers and stick-pushers as preventative measures.
